subject: Cloud Computing
title: Netflix: The Cloud Migration Story
description: One-minute skill: Netflix: The Cloud Migration Story.

hook.text: In 2008, Netflix's data center failed and DVDs couldn't ship for three days. That was the last straw.

buildup.text: Netflix decided to move everything to AWS. The migration took seven years to complete.

discovery.text: They built Chaos Monkey, a tool that randomly kills servers to test if the system survives.

twist.text: Netflix now runs entirely on a competitor's cloud. Amazon sells cloud and streams video.

climax.text: Netflix proved that even massive, critical services could run reliably in the public cloud.

punchline.text: Netflix trusts Amazon's cloud. Even though they compete.

quiz.question: What was Netflix's Chaos Monkey designed to do?
options: Randomly kill servers to test system resilience
Monitor customer viewing habits for recommendations
Compress video files for faster streaming

details.summary: Netflix migrated completely from its own data centers to AWS over seven years, finishing in 2016. The migration pioneered cloud architecture patterns including microservices, chaos engineering, and multi-region resilience that the entire industry later adopted.
details.whyItMatters: Netflix's migration proved that even the most demanding applications could run entirely in the cloud. Their open-source tools and architecture patterns became blueprints for the industry.
takeaways: Netflix took seven years to fully migrate to AWS
They pioneered microservices and chaos engineering in the cloud
Their open-source tools became industry-standard patterns

faq.question: Why did Netflix migrate to the cloud?
faq.answer: A major database corruption in 2008 caused a three-day shipping outage that convinced Netflix to move away from single points of failure. As they shifted from DVD shipping to streaming, cloud scalability became essential for handling traffic spikes during popular releases.

faq.question: What did Netflix contribute to cloud computing?
faq.answer: Netflix open-sourced dozens of cloud tools including Chaos Monkey for resilience testing, Zuul for API routing, and Eureka for service discovery. Their architecture patterns for microservices, circuit breakers, and multi-region failover became industry best practices.
